title: Regional fallback regret minimizer: notes and decision tree
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is an engineering sketch for a compact, operational decision tree that prioritizes routes across regions and model variants by minimizing expected regret (utility loss) rather than only optimizing for a single metric. Goal: make routing choices that balance tail latency, unit cost, and probability of success (reliability) in a way that is robust to noisy signals and abrupt capacity changes.

Context / motivation:
- We have many compatible model variants (quantized, fp16, distilled) and multiple regions with different capacity profiles and cost bases.
- Existing heuristics often flip aggressively when latency or cost crosses a threshold, causing oscillation and increased error rates.
- Minimizing expected regret gives a softer preference structure: pick a route that would have performed near-best in most plausible scenarios, rather than the single best under current noisy measurements.

High-level idea (plain language):
1) For each candidate route (region+variant), maintain 3 short-term exponential moving estimates: median latency, tail p95+ latency, and success_rate (fraction of requests that complete without fallback). Also maintain unit_cost_estimate (dollars per 1k tokens) and a small regression score for quality (inferred from eval set or production A/B).
2) Translate these dimensions into a single utility distribution via simple parametric noise model (we treat measured latency as mean of a normal with sigma derived from p95 - median; treat cost as log-normal with small sigma; treat reliability as Bernoulli with Beta posterior).
3) Compute expected utility for each route and the expected regret relative to the (unknown) optimal. Use an approx: sample N=50 draws from the utility distributions and compute regret per route.
4) Apply hysteresis and rollout budgets: only switch primary route when the expected regret reduction exceeds a configurable threshold and the route has sustained advantage for T_sustain seconds or N_samples requests.

Utility specification (engineering form):
- Utility U = - (w_latency * latency_ms_normalized + w_cost * unit_cost_normalized - w_rel * reliability_bonus + w_quality_penalty * quality_delta_normalized)
- Normalize terms to [0,1] using running min/max per-candidate over a sliding window (1h).
- We treat reliability as a bonus (higher is better) so subtracting a negative improves utility.
- We tune weights at rollout time per-customer or per-route class. Example weights: w_latency=0.5, w_cost=0.3, w_rel=0.4, w_quality_penalty=0.6 (these don't sum to 1; utility is arbitrary scale).

Uncertainty model (practical):
- latency ~ Normal(mu=median_latency, sigma = clipped((p95 - median)/1.5, min=10ms, max=300ms))
- cost ~ LogNormal(mu=log(unit_cost), sigma=0.1)
- reliability ~ Beta(alpha=successes+1, beta=failures+1) -> sample probability
- quality_delta (measured score delta vs baseline) ~ Normal(mu=observed_delta, sigma=abs(observed_delta)*0.5 + small_eps)

Sampling/approx regret algorithm (pseudocode in words):
- candidates = all region+variant routes that satisfy compatibility and blacklists
- for i in 1..N_samples (N=50):
  - for each candidate c: draw u_c^(i) from utility distribution using the above models
  - pick best_i = argmax_c u_c^(i)
- for each candidate c: compute regret_c = mean_i( u_best_i^(i) - u_c^(i) )
- choose route = argmin_c regret_c subject to hysteresis and rollout constraints

Operational constraints and heuristics:
- Safety blacklist: routes that have had > X failures in last Y minutes or are under incident are removed
- Soft-capacity damping: when a route is near capacity (utilization>80%), multiply latency sigma by 1.5 to reflect higher variability and thus increase regret for that candidate
- Cost floors: if route.unit_cost > cost_floor_for_customer, prefer cheaper route unless reliability_gain > reliability_threshold
- Warm-start bias: prefer current primary by adding small bias_b_current to its sampled utility until sustain timer expires (reduces flip-flop)
- Canary/rollout policy: allow N_canary concurrent requests (small fraction) to trial a lower-regret route before promoting

Hysteresis and promotion rules (practical knobs):
- promote if expected_regret(current) - expected_regret(candidate) > delta_regret_threshold AND candidate.sustained_count >= N_sustain
- delta_regret_threshold default = 0.02 (utility units) — tuned empirically
- N_sustain default = min(500, RPS * 30s)

Decision tree sketch (textual) — entry point when new request arrives:
1) Gather candidate set (filter: model compatibility, region allowed, legal/data locality)
2) Exclude blacklisted routes (incidents, outdated models)
3) Compute short-term stats and normalize
4) Run regret sampling -> get regret scores per-candidate
5) Rank by regret asc -> top K (K=3)
6) If top candidate == current_primary: send request there (unless capacity triggers fallback)
7) Else if top candidate in canary_pool and canary_quota available: send as canary
8) Else if top candidate passes delta_regret_threshold and sustained checks: promote and route
9) Else route to current_primary

Examples (toy):
- Region A (fp16): median 40ms, p95 120ms, success 0.995, cost 0.8x
- Region B (int8): median 60ms, p95 100ms, success 0.985, cost 0.4x
- Using weights above and sampling, Region A may have slightly better mean utility but higher tail variance. If a burst occurs, sampling reveals Region B has lower regret due to cost and tighter tail -> chosen for many requests.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Oscillation between two equal routes: mitigate with larger bias_b_current and increase N_sustain, or use exponential backoff on switches.
- Measurement staleness: ensure p95 and median use short windows for production (1–5 min) with fallback to longer windows if insufficient samples.
- Overfitting to early data: add minimum sample counts before using route for primary (min_samples=100)

Telemetry and observability (must have):
- Per-route: median, p95, success_rate, unit_cost_est, traffic_fraction, regret_score, sigma_latency
- Events: route_switch, canary_promote, route_blacklist, sustained_threshold_cross
- Dashboards: regret by route over time, switch frequency, switch-related error spikes

Operational checklist for rollout:
- Step 0: instrument per-route metrics and ensure <2s metric lag
- Step 1: run offline sim for 2 weeks using production traces to measure switch rate and tail risk
- Step 2: enable sampling-only mode (no actual routing change, only compute decisions) for 48h
- Step 3: enable 1% canary traffic, monitor errors & latency for 2h, if stable increase to 10%
- Step 4: enable promotion with conservative delta_regret_threshold and long N_sustain, monitor 24h

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How to integrate route-level model-quality signals that arrive at slower cadence? Proposed: decouple quality_delta into slower-weighted term in utility (lower weight) and refresh it from nightly evals.
- Best default hyperparameters for different customer classes (low-latency consumer apps vs batch embed jobs)
- Should we use Thompson-sampling style exploration explicitly, or is the regret-sampling approximating that sufficiently? (tradeoffs: exploration noise vs production stability)

Immediate next steps (short):
- Rafael: add simulation harness to replay one week of prod traffic and compute switch frequency under default knobs (due 2024-03-12)
- Ava: instrument per-route p95/median drift metrics in telemetry pipeline (due 2024-03-07)
- Marcus: prototype sampling/regret compute in a small service and expose decision logs (due 2024-03-15)

Quick notes to self (informal):
- Keep the sampling N small (50) to bound CPU. If many candidates, prefilter by coarse heuristic (top-6 by mean utility) then sample.
- Add simple budget accounting: when a cheap region is used too much, start penalizing its unit_cost_normalized (internal fairness across fleets).
- Document failure scenarios where regret approach can be gamed by transient success spikes.

References and inspiration:
- bandit/regret literature (Auer et al.) and Thompson sampling notes
- internal incident postmortems where oscillation between regions caused higher error budgets

End of document.
